utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. And good morning, everybody. All the accused are here. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer. Do you see anyone else there? I can't see. Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. Defence teams, we are okay. All right, full house today. Any preliminaries? Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, at some point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, at some point, the Gvero Defence would like to make an application for our client to make a further Rule 84 bis statement. I'm unclear whether the Trial Chamber would like me to do that today, prior to the Prosecution beginning their closing arguments, or whether the Trial Chamber would rather we did that at some point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Later, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll try -- in fact, that brings me to the only thing that I wanted to say before we start; that it is the Trial Chamber's preference that during the various interventions - today we start with the Prosecution submissions - there will be no interruptions from the other side unless it is a procedural issue or something of such importance that would warrant the interruption. You will then have ample opportunity later on to make your submissions to say whatever you want to say. But we'll come to you later on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm ready to make the application whenever it suits the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you ought to start thinking about it and have it ready. Okay, thank you. Mr. McCloskey, have you decided how to divide the work between you or is it just going to be you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Excuse me, let me just try out this new position a bit. I'm strangling myself. Yes, we have, and it will be -- you're taking me out of my prepared comments, which is just as well, but it will -- I will make a few brief comments. Then I will turn the case over to Mr. Thayer, who will discuss the case against Miletic and Gvero. Then Mr. Vanderpuye will discuss the case against Popovic and Beara. Then we will have Chris Mitchell discuss the case against Drago Nikolic. Rupert Elderkin will speak of the opportunistic crimes. Lada Soljan will speak briefly regarding the destruction of the women and children and some of the forensic issues. And I will end with a discussion on the cases against Mr. Borovcanin and General Pandurevic. That is our plan, and we hope to take less than the time given, though we'll have to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. That also means that whenever the previous speaker comes to an end, the next one ought to be prepared to start straight away. So keep that in mind, that we're not going to have the rest of the day off simply because you prefer to continue or to start the day after. So be ready for that. Yes. So let's start. Basically, the timing -- Registrar, the time that we allowed the Prosecution for its submissions, the nine hours or whatever they are, starts from now. Okay. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my colleagues, it has been a real honour and a privilege to appear before you all these three years. I speak for myself and I speak for my entire team. For over three years, this Trial Chamber has conducted this trial with the utmost professionalism, integrity, patience and, yes, calm, and with myself on the late evenings of the later days and some of us and my colleagues, that, as you know, was not an easy task. Your concentration and your attention to detail was noticed immediately by all parties, and you put us on notice right off that day in and day out our words, the words of the witnesses, would be heard, would be considered, would never be taken lightly, and would have significance. This is greatly appreciated by all of us. You let us try our case. You let the Defence try our case. There's no stopwatches in this trial and in this courtroom for three years, and I can't tell you how much I appreciate that, personally. Had it been tried another way, I think we would have collapsed long ago. We greatly appreciate the way this Trial Chamber conducted this trial. We also, of course, appreciate and thank the interpreters and their difficult job, the court reporters. The court reporters and interpreters take a lot of guff in these trials, and they did a fabulous job; and the entire courtroom, the Registry, everyone. Thank you very much. I thank my colleagues for conducting themselves. We came through this as colleagues and more than that, and that's not easily said in a trial of this length and depth. Now, I just have a few words before turning the case over to Mr. Thayer for his initial comments, and I want to remind you of a couple of themes that I discussed in the opening statement that I think, after looking at the Defence case and reading their briefs, are as important now, if not more so, than when I first brought them up. The first topic I'd like to mention briefly is that of proving specific intent. Specific intent is the intent set out in the Statute, be it an intent to destroy in whole or in part a group because of their ethnicity or some other particular object set out in a particular Statute. The law of the Tribunal does not require the Prosecution to prove that accused acted with desire or conscious desire to commit the crime, but he must have acted with the specific intent for many of the Statutes. But what is specific intent, if it is not necessarily the desire to achieve the illegal goal? Now, in my view and in my history, legal history, specific intent is willful conduct done intentionally, not by accident or unconsciously, with the knowledge that such conduct will achieve or provide substantial assistance in achieving a criminal end, be it murder, destruction of a group, in whole or in part, the forcible removal. Now, this is where my discussion of duty came in in the opening statement. I remind you that the officers in this case are all creatures and trained in their duty. And as I've said before, perhaps the most important job on this earth. These are the people, the armed forces, that protect our homes and our families when it's under dire threat. They are operated by the duty to follow the Geneva Conventions, the duty to follow their own regulations, the duty not to commit criminal conduct. So for each of these men to be guilty of these crimes, in my view, they had to do three things, three distinct things that went through their mind in order to get where we have today. The first thing they had to do was disregard their duty. They knew what they had to do when they get posed with criminal orders, criminal events, they know it's not -- they have to stand down. They know that. The first thing they do in the road to criminal conduct is they disregard that consciously. They consciously make the decision to disregard their duty, disregard the law. The next thing they do is they fail to sabotage the crime or to help the victims, like Schindler did. They had the opportunity, all of these men did, when they heard this, to call up ICRC secretly, if they wanted, bring in a reporter, call in the UNHCR, go to Mendeljev Djuric and say, Stop that, do not separate those men. They made the conscious decision not to do any of that. They could have. I know Vinko Pandurevic has the will and the guts to do just that. We got to know each other from this case. He could have. He chose not to. The third thing and the most important thing is they made the choice to participate. They made the choice to step forward and take part in this awful, awful conduct. Now, the second theme related to that is we saw from the trial briefs, and we've seen through the Defence case, the Defence focuses on the executions, the privates pulling the triggers, or in the context of the forcible transfer, the Potocari. These crimes are so much more than that. Frankly, we have seen the Tribunal and the law of the Tribunal over the years focus on the act of a bullet passing through the body of a person as the ultimate commission. Well, I disagree with that. That is part of the crime. But more importantly and just as equally are the organising that goes into the crime, the planning, the transporting, the capturing, the detaining, yes, the shooting, the burying, and the hiding. I call the reburial the hiding. This is part of murder. So when you see Borovcanin, for example, suggest over and over again, I'm not in Potocari, I'm not in Potocari during any of the crimes, well, he's in command of the units that are in Potocari, he's involved in all the critical other details that I've talked about, including the critical details, the same with Vinko Pandurevic. The only time we see a commander at a mass execution is when one of his men gets killed or it burns his hand. Otherwise, they're in the IKM, they're in their vehicle, they've got their Motorola. That's where these crimes are the most heinous, in my view. When Vinko Pandurevic and General Radislav Krstic are sitting together at the IKM in Zepa, clearly discussing what's going on in Zvornik so Pandurevic can be prepared, this is where Pandurevic needed to step up and say, No, I'm going to order my men to put those people on buses and send them to Batkovic. He could have done that. That didn't happen. They got their act together to get the job done that they needed to get done, in their view. So, please, when you see these crimes, look at them in the completeness that they are, not the act of the executions only or the horrendous thing of putting people on buses. In any event, you have heard from me for so long, and I certainly know that you appreciate the understanding and the knowledge of my colleagues and their professionalism, and I think it's time for me to turn over the podium to Nelson Thayer to talk about Generals Miletic and Gvero. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you looking at the clock. We'll have a break at 10.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. I will address the evidence concerning Generals Miletic and Gvero, as Mr. McCloskey mentioned, and I will try to heed the Trial Chamber's advice to stick to matters that were left out of our trial brief for some reason or that were raised in someone else's trial brief that we feel we need to respond to in some manner, as opposed to rehashing all of our themes over again. In responding, at the outset, to some of the arguments which overlap, understandably, between the Gvero and Miletic trial briefs, I'll necessarily address some of their conduct and contributions together, although I will be presenting -- making submissions separately afterwards. Because of the way we are responding, more than rehashing, there'll be some jumping back and forth. There might be a little hodge-podge nature here or there, because we're pulling different pieces of information that we want to bring to the Court's attention or deal with. So please bear with me and, I dare say so, my colleagues, as we proceed. I want to address, Your Honours, first a couple of propositions made in the Miletic brief; namely, at page 153, paragraph 356: "The objective was not to expel the Muslim populations from the Drina Valley, but rather to create the conditions necessary to make it possible for the Muslim population to stay." I'd like to address that, as well as a related proposition in the Miletic brief at page 154, paragraph 358: "It is not certain that the Army of the Republic of Srpska ever implemented the strategic objectives in its orders." Your Honours, to the contrary, the evidence has been overwhelming that the Krivaja 95 and Stupcanica 95 operations were the culmination of the Bosnian Serb efforts to implement the strategic objectives and to expel the Muslim populations from Srebrenica and Zepa pursuant to those objectives. I'm not going to repeat our sections in the brief on these issues at paragraphs 18 to 97 and 212 to 281, for example, but I would like to recall certain VRS orders that explicitly did implement the strategic objectives to remove the Muslim population from Srebrenica and Zepa. And I want to first take you for a moment back to 1992, September 2nd, a major meeting in Bijeljina among political and military leaders, where the gospel of ethnic separation is being spread. General Gvero represents the VRS. Karadzic and Krajisnik are there. The gathered are addressed. And as well there is the East Bosnia Corps commander, then Colonel Ivica Simic, who listens to Krajisnik's recitation of the strategic objectives, the first of which Colonel Simic faithfully records as separation from the Muslims. 19 November 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you referring to any specific document that is on record?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I'm referring to the war diary of General Simic. I'm afraid I don't have that cite handy for you. I can certainly get that for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please do, because it is something that might be important for the interested party to reply to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have the Main Staff's directive, 19 November 1992, Directive 4, Exhibit P29, containing the criminal order to force out the Muslim civilian population from Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde. Some four days later, 23 November 1992, there is a political/military seminar in Zvornik. General Gvero, of course, is there, and Directive 4, the evidence has established, must have been discussed there. Among those present include, in addition to General Gvero, General Krstic, Rajko Kusic, Vinko Pandurevic. That line-up may sound familiar. All of those officers we see July 26th, 1995, in the Boksanica video, as the Muslim population of Zepa is being forcibly removed from that enclave. That gives you an idea of how truly small this family of brothers-in-arms was, Your Honours, and keep in mind that, in particular, the Main Staff was not some sprawling bureaucracy. It was a small, self-selected group of officers, professionally trained officers, who served together through the war, shoulder to shoulder in some cases; in the case of General Miletic and his colleagues, at the command post in Crna Rijeka, with Generals Mladic, Tolimir, and Gvero in the field, as we've seen time and again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your reference for this meeting of the 23rd of November, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, that is the testimony of Novica -- pardon me, Your Honour. That's discussed in two places in the brief, Your Honour. Again, I can get you those cites. It's discussed in the -- in the beginning portion as well as in the Pandurevic section, and I can get you those paragraphs. When speaking about the Main Staff, Your Honours, again keep in mind General Gvero was one of only four generals among the founding officers of the VRS Main Staff, along with Generals Mladic, Milovanovic and Djukic. Then Colonel Miletic joined the Main Staff just a short time later in July of 1992. Now, back to the VRS orders. Following Directive 4, following the military/political seminar in Zvornik. On 24 November, 1992, General Zivanovic, the commander of the newly formed Drina Corps, issues order number 2-126, that's Exhibit P03029. Again, an acknowledged criminal order following that seminar, explicitly referencing Directive 4, ordering the forcible removal of the Muslim population from Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde. And what followed was the Drina Corps's brutal ethnic cleansing campaign targeting the Muslim populations and culminating in the creation of the Srebrenica safe area. And I won't repeat what's in our brief at paragraphs 72 to 83 and again in the Pandurevic section of the brief at paragraphs 1281 to 1324. It's important to note, Your Honours, that the Main Staff understood that campaign as a significant step towards realising Strategic Objective Number 3, the elimination of the Drina River as a border between Serb states. I want to turn your attention to Exhibit P00414, which is the 1992 combat readiness analysis report, which as you may recall is actually promulgated in 1993 because it's a retroactive sort of report card done by the VRS itself. At page 160, I quote: "The analysis finds by taking Kamenica, Cerska, Glogova, the region of Osmace village and Jadar, the Drina Corps has considerably expanded the free territory and will shortly have achieved the strategic task assigned to it by the Supreme Command, while at the same time providing protection for the Serbian people." Now, these are not, as I said, the words of some politician somewhere. This assessment of the success towards the realisation of Strategic Objective 3, these are the words of General Miletic's immediate supervisor/commanding officer at the time, the chief of operations and training, Dragutin Ilic, who signs the analysis report at page 164. And it's important to note here, if you take a look at the passage I just read, there's a distinction made by the Main Staff analysis between the forcible removal, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, the protection of the Serbian people which, when you read the analysis, refers to protection from genocide and terrorism against the Serbs by Muslims and Croats, which is what General Gvero is reinforcing to the rank and file. These are two vital but distinct ideas, interrelated but distinct; the removal as a strategic objective, protection of the Serbian people as a more public and publicly-acknowledged objective. Now, General Miletic, himself, helped implement Directive 4 and Strategic Objective 3 during his Operation Spring 93, which is described in more detail at paragraph 1664 of our brief. In short, Spring 93 was a combat operation designed to liberate the Zepa and Gorazde enclaves. The language General Miletic used in that combat order is telling, and I quote: "To crush and destroy Muslim armed formations in the broader area of Zepa and Gorazde, and to enable the Muslim civilian population to move out." In parentheses he's written: "(Transfer to other territories.)" Again in parentheses: "(Central part of the former BiH.)" "... or to recognise the rule of Republika Srpska and in that manner create conditions for the return of the Serbian population to the left and right bank of the Drina River." That's Exhibit P02742, page 6. Again, explicit references to the strategic objectives. Miletic was on the ground, coordinating the fighting during this operation, which stopped only because Zepa was declared a safe area. So it's no wonder that former Main Staff operations officer Colonel Miljenko Lasic spoke so candidly to Your Honours and appeared to take it so much for granted when he spoke about the role of the VRS in separating the Bosnian people ethnically. And that's at transcript 21833 to 21835. And, Your Honours, the focus on these unrealised strategic objectives of removing the Muslim population and eliminating the Drina as a border, and I say "unrealised" because the Srebrenica safe area put the brake on that, that remained unrealised but pursued. In July of 1994, President Karadzic addressed the Bosnian Serb Assembly and stated loud and clear, and I quote: "Our primary strategic aim, which is to get rid of the enemies in our house, the Croats and the Muslims, and not to be in the same state with them anymore." And again, finally, following the elimination of the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, in August of 1995 President Karadzic is still referring to the strategic objectives, the Drina corridor, and how strategically important it was for Srebrenica, which he admitted was a Muslim territory, to become Serb. And that's at P03307, pages 68 to 69. With respect to those initial propositions that I quoted from the Miletic brief, Your Honours, the evidence has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the VRS rigorously enforced and implemented Directive 4 and the strategic objectives on the ground in the Podrinje Valley. The system worked in 1995, as it did in 1992, with the supreme commander, Radovan Karadzic, working in close cooperation with the VRS Main Staff, setting forth his priorities and goals, and the Main Staff executing those and implementing them on the ground. Now, what I'd like to do is turn to some additional arguments made in the Miletic brief concerning Directive 7. Specifically, Your Honours, at page 65, paragraph 164, and page 67, paragraph 169, I quote from the brief: "Nobody can exclude the possibility that General Miletic did not agree with the final text of Directive 7, and that he effectively expressed his disagreement in such a way that he would have removed him from the finalisation of Directive 7 --" pardon me, "that would have removed him from the finalisation of Directive 7." Your Honours, there is no evidence on this record that that happened; none. And, again, page 67, paragraph 168, the proposition is put that the possibility remains that President Karadzic added the illegal language to Directive 7 before signing it, and after General Miletic gave it to him. Again, there is no evidence on this record that anything like that happened. To the contrary, Your Honours, the evidence has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that General Miletic and General Gvero each participated in the drafting of and implementing of Directive 7. With respect to General Miletic's role in drafting Directive 7, and we've addressed that in our brief at paragraph 1669 to 1678, we know he saw the final draft before it went to President Karadzic. General Miletic's name is on it. General Miletic finalised it. General Simic testified to that. General Miletic specifically referred to Directive 7 a few weeks later, when he drafted Directive 7(1). General Miletic had a copy of the final version in his strong box. And, lastly, General Miletic implemented it. Now, when General Miletic's name appears at the end of a document like Directive 7, that means something. When you see it just above President Karadzic's signature, it means, as we've set forth in the brief, that he's read it and that he approves it, he takes responsibility for it. He puts his professional approval to it and, particularly with respect to Directive 7, I dare say, his professional pride in it. I do want to note that there is an error in paragraph 1675 of our brief. The reference to paragraph 1636 in that paragraph 1675 should actually be a reference to paragraphs 113 and 114. So we gave you a bum cite there. In any event, Your Honours, the Miletic brief concedes, as it must, that General Miletic was familiar with the final version of Directive 7. Of course he was familiar with it. He had to know it inside-out. He was responsible for putting it together. That document had to faithfully reflect and implement the overall strategic war aims and make military sense. President Karadzic might have had his big ideas, he might have thought he was a military man, but he wasn't. So it was up to the Main Staff to implement those ideas on the ground. And General Miletic doesn't just cut-and-paste and stitch together these various pieces of information that are coming in to him during the process of drafting this critical document. He can't do that. Professionally, he wouldn't do that, because he has to integrate all of these various pieces of information and direction into a whole that makes military sense, that's militarily feasible, that is accurate and accurately reflects the situation in the war theatre at the time. Karadzic and his people can't do that. The person who is most singularly prepared and capable of doing that was General Miletic, and for that reason he was invested with such trust by Generals Mladic and Milovanovic. Now, the evidence is -- has been established beyond a reasonable doubt that the full method or the complete method was used for the drafting of this directive, and I'm going to recite again this critical language from section 6.1, that: "The relevant state and military organs responsible for the work with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistic support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Bosnian Muslim population, making them dependent on our goodwill, while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and international public opinion." This passage recognises that this has to be done, in its own words, unobtrusively. The VRS understood that it could not impose an absolute blockade on the enclaves without drawing fire from the international community for it, and the evidence shows that this language was provided by General Gvero's organ. First, it appears under the section headed "Moral and Psychological Support." And it includes morale-related directions for information and propaganda activities to be coordinated with the state, and raising awareness of the soldiers and populous of the arms struggle. And, second, as we've argued in our brief, of all the Main Staff assistant commanders, it was General Gvero who constantly had his eye on the international and diplomatic scene and upon international public opinion. Now, the section containing the direction to the Drina Corps: "To create an unbearable situation of total insecurity, with no hope for further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa," and the section I just read to you about the convoys, were illegal. General Miletic had a duty to say, Wait a minute, no, I will not. And General Miletic recognises this duty in his brief at pages 67 to 68, paragraph 170. He concedes his duty, and I quote from the brief: "The only solution available to General Miletic, if he disagreed with Directive 7, was to inform his superiors and General Milovanovic in the first instance." Of course, that wasn't the only solution, Your Honours, but it was his duty in the first instance. And instead, General Miletic proceeded to rigorously implement those illegal portions of Directive 7 to strangle the eastern enclaves, with the ultimate objective of removing the Muslim population from them. Your Honours, the Momir Nikolics of this world don't just suddenly get the bright idea to clamp down on the humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR convoys coming into their area of responsibility, to search pursuant to very particularised directions ever convoy. They get orders to do that. They get orders to do that from the General Miletics of this world. And we saw in the Bratunac Brigade mid-year combat readiness analysis report in July 1995 that it had set up the check-point and was operating it pursuant to Main Staff orders, and that's Exhibit 4D00316. Yes, restrictions were in place from practically the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 4D00316, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But the convoy restrictions were tightened and tightened and tightened further pursuant to Directive 7 in order to bring the situation in the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves to a boiling point. I won't recite all of the DutchBat testimony you heard, all the other testimony that's in our brief. Again, yes, there were restrictions, there had always been restrictions, but the evidence was loud and clear that the VRS tightened those restrictions considerably beginning in March and April of 1995, and those restrictions had a devastating effect on DutchBat's operability and the humanitarian situation in the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. And, Your Honours, the criminal nature of those passages is only underscored by General Milovanovic's less-than-candid testimony about them. I think we dinged General Milovanovic a little bit in our brief about not being completely candid with respect to Directive 4, and we would urge the same caution with respect to his testimony regarding not being familiar with Directive 7 or 7(1). His lack of memory speaks volumes about his recognition of the obvious; that those words mean what they say on the paper, and they were brutal in practice. I want to address an additional comment -- comment to both briefs, and that is that some of the Muslim population already wished to leave Srebrenica and Zepa by July 1995. Both teams rely, for example, on 5D00259. That is a written plea from May 1995, from Hodja Mehmed Hajric, who you may or may not recall was the hodja in Zepa. He was head of the War Presidency as well. You saw a still image of him with a notepad in his hand, trying to regulate somehow the forcible removal of his fellow Zepans on 25 July 1995. His remains were found in a mass grave, along with Amir Imamovic, one of the negotiators who met with the VRS during the course of the VRS attack on the enclave. In any event, in May of 1995 Mr. Hajric wrote to the armija, to the ABiH, to arrange with the VRS, he hoped, a welfare evacuation because of the poor living conditions in Zepa at the time. He points out in this document that the Muslim women, children, and elderly who had been ethnically cleansed into Zepa, of which there are many, were seeking to relocate elsewhere because they didn't have enough food and the living conditions were so poor. A similar document cited by the Defence, 6D00047, refers to people leaving Srebrenica, heading for Zepa to look for food. Now, I just want to say that in accusing the Muslim authorities, as both briefs go on to do, for wanting to keep their Muslim citizens within these enclaves and not permit the mass exodus of suffering people, to somehow accuse and place the blame on those Muslim authorities, the Defence utterly ignores the simple fact that the VRS created those very conditions through Directive 7, and that's been the evidence in this case from Day 1, Your Honours. I want to jump ahead chronologically, Your Honours, and this is one of those places where it's just a little helter-skelter because I need to address an issue that's common to both accused. At page 150, paragraph 346 of the Miletic brief, there is the proposition that Miletic had nothing to do with the transportation of Muslims from Potocari during the period of 17 to 19 July. Richard Butler testified about these events and the related documents on 17 January 2008, and that's at transcript 19909 to 910 and 19921 to 36. And we didn't go into great detail at all in our brief about this series of events, but I do want to talk a little bit more about it, given the Miletic brief's discussion of it. You may recall basically what we have during this period of time, the transportations from Potocari are over, you've got a Main Staff intelligence officer, Radoslav Jankovic, who has been based at the Bratunac Brigade Command, and he's also on the ground in Potocari in the period following the fall of the enclave. You've heard testimony about Colonel Jankovic from, among others, Colonel Franken, the DutchBat deputy commanding officer, and you've seen documents going out under Colonel Jankovic's name, most recently during the testimony of Momir Nikolic, whose testimony was, I believe, uncontested with respect to those reports from Colonel Jankovic. So we have the issue remaining during these days of some wounded who are waiting to be taken out of the enclave, and that's what General Gvero was dealing with with the ICRC and UNHCR, and we discuss that in our brief at paragraphs 1808 through 1816. And one thing that I want to add that we neglected to cite in our brief in that section is P02567. Again, that's P02567. That is a convoy notification which states that VRS representatives, on 16 July, met with ICRC and UNHCR representatives, and that, Your Honours, confirms the evidence that we have summarised in our brief; that General Gvero did, in fact, meet with representatives of both agencies on that day, and there are numerous documents which support that on either end. Now, paragraph 385 of the Gvero brief suggests that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. You're using a -- or you started this part of your intervention by referring to a specific part of the Miletic brief, namely, page 150, para 346, but used it then to point your finger towards General Gvero. Now, you've said nothing as regards General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm getting there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is -- as I said, this is one of those incidents where they are intertwined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- so I'll be discussing them both at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to General Gvero's involvement with transporting these wounded out of Bratunac, the Gvero brief suggests that Koljevic's state committee controlled these events, and they offer an exhibit which was recently admitted, 6D00348, which notes a 15 July meeting between a UN civil affairs officer and Professor Koljevic, in which Professor Koljevic signs an order for the evacuation of those wounded from Bratunac. Naturally, the Gvero brief places the responsibility then for that transportation upon Professor Koljevic and not General Gvero and the Main Staff. However, when we take a look at the convoy approval that is issued by General Miletic, as with all the other convoy approvals that we've seen, it's the VRS, the Main Staff, which holds the ultimate power to decide whether or not a convoy is going to pass, with how many vehicles, with what goods, on what date, all the particulars are all reposed in the VRS. Koljevic and his state committee might make some kind of an initial approval, but it always goes to the Main Staff, and they have the power to say yes or no. And that convoy notification states, naturally: "We have approved the transportation." And again it refers to this meeting on 16 July between the VRS and ICRC and UNHCR. And those wounded Muslims didn't get evacuated when Nikola Koljevic -- Professor Koljevic signed that order. The ball got rolling when General Gvero sat down and met with those agencies. Now, back to Colonel Jankovic in Potocari. He's in a quandary. They've evacuated some of these wounded, but they still have Muslim staff members of, for example, MSF, and he doesn't know what's supposed to be done with them. Do the men get separated, do they all go out with MSF, is there an escort? He doesn't know. Do they get detained? The Miletic brief notes that on 17 July, and this is at page 150, paragraph 347, and I quote: "Colonel Jankovic is requested to send his requests to General Tolimir, who would determine the matter with the commander." And what the brief leaves out is that it is General Miletic who is the one telling Jankovic to put his submission in writing to General Tolimir, encoded. And we have an intercept that reflects just that, P01237A. And sure enough, the next day, 18 July, Jankovic sends his inquiry to Tolimir. That's P00260. And then at the other end we have General Miletic again issuing another approval for the transportation the following day, 19 July, with a notation to Momir Nikolic, Basically don't let those NGO people out of your sight. That's P02570. Basically, what the Miletic brief ignores is that General Miletic, as I said, is at both ends of this very specific removal of these Muslims from the enclave, as part of the forcible transfer operation, and the associated need to keep the NGOs' movement restricted because, as he well knows, as everyone knows by this time, north of Bratunac is a crime scene. It is also reflective of Miletic fundamentally receiving a request from Jankovic and, in his singular role at the Main Staff, being able to properly direct Jankovic to where Jankovic needs to go. Miletic knows very well what he's capable of taking care of and what he's not. And you'll see in that intercept that he tells the caller, Tell Jankovic he's got to put everything in writing, get it to Tolimir, get it there encoded. And that gets the ball rolling. On a related issue, the Gvero brief claims that the transportation of the wounded Muslims from Bratunac was not forced - that's at page 248 - paragraph 370, and states in support of that proposition that: "On 12 July, patients were brought from the Srebrenica Hospital to the DutchBat compound during the attack because treatment at the former was not as good or as advanced as it was in the DutchBat compound. Also, there was an MSF hospital in the DutchBat compound." And they cite Colonel Kingori's testimony for that proposition. I submit that's not an entirely accurate citation. MSF was located at the DutchBat compound on 12 July because it had been shelled out of the Srebrenica Hospital the day before. DutchBat officer Egbers testified without contradiction that he helped evacuate the hospital patients on 11 July. That's at transcript 2717 to 2719. Colonel Boering also testified about his soldiers accompanying the flow of refugees and that they also evacuated the hospital, when MSF told him -- told DutchBat that it was too dangerous for them to stay. That's at transcript 1931 and 1937. And then PW-105 told you the circumstances under which he left the hospital, and I won't go any further. I'd like to turn now to another proposition in the Miletic brief at page 72, paragraph 182, that there never existed any plan to deliberately restrict humanitarian aid to the enclaves in Eastern Bosnia. And, again, I'm not going to repeat the extensive evidence of just such a plan, and I'll just direct Your Honours' attention to paragraphs 215 to 245 of our brief and, in particular, to paragraph 238, which describes the reality experienced by UNHCR on the ground in Srebrenica the first week of July 1995. And the fact is that the amounts that were being delivered were for minimum survival subsistence levels, so you can imagine -- well, you don't have to imagine, you can recall the testimony, the evidence, of all the witness as to what even a 10 per cent decrease would be. And, again, the VRS didn't have to impose a complete blockade on the food and humanitarian aid. They just had to turn the heat up a little bit and a little bit and a little bit to really make a difference, because the situation was so poor. Now, I do want to address some of the citations. First, there's a claim that convoys to Serb communities received the same treatment as the convoys that were going, for example, to Srebrenica and Zepa, and one example that's used is 5D00856, which shows convoys going to Vlasenica, Sokolac, Visegrad, Bratunac. And I just note that when you look at what's going, first of all, nothing's getting denied. It's all going; flour, 25.000 litres of diesel, barrels of fuel. So I don't think that example really holds up to scrutiny. And at page 105, paragraph 246 of the brief, it refers to an NGO report which is under seal, so I'm going to be very careful and try to stay in public session. I'm not going to quote from it, but the exhibit number is 5D01446. The Miletic brief cites this report for the proposition that there were adequate medical supplies in Potocari in July of 1995. Suffice it to say that it's the Prosecution's submission that when you look at this report, it is, quite to the contrary, evidence that only by the late afternoon of July 13th there was no need for any medicine anymore, as recognised in this report, because there was, in the words of the report, zero people expected to be left. The Miletic brief also states at paragraph 123 -- I'm sorry, page 123, paragraph 282: "Restrictions imposed upon UNPROFOR convoys had no bearing upon humanitarian aid transported to the enclaves, as this aid was ferried by humanitarian organisation convoys." Now, that may be true in a most hyper-technical sense, but the evidence was clear that Srebrenica depended upon DutchBat's medical assistance, medical support. And please look at page 76, paragraph 245 of our brief, and I would simply quote briefly from P00510, an UNMO report from 11 July at 1730 hours, as the refugees are streaming in, and this is after MSF has been shelled up to the compound: "DutchBat can't give much help because their supplies have not been coming in since the end of April. The only medical help that is available is coming from MSF. However, that is also not enough for all the wounded people." The Miletic brief also concedes that, and I quote: "The refusal to authorise the return of DutchBat members certainly had an influence on its ability to correctly fulfill its mission, yet it did not affect the humanitarian situation with the enclave." The evidence is so overwhelming, Your Honours, that if DutchBat had had more men, more fuel, of course it could have affected the humanitarian situation in the enclave. They would have done more patrols. With 600 men instead of 300, they, of course, would have had more of a presence in 1995. They could have mounted a stronger defence had they had fresh ammunition, sufficient weapons, weapons systems, equipment that worked, and, of course, with more control over the compound, just one of many things that would have been different were the opportunistic killings, would certainly have been fewer. Now, I want to turn to some other portion of the Miletic brief, just hit on a few things. At page 156, paragraph 363, the brief makes the point that: "It was not unusual for the population to withdraw from a given territory along with the armed forces, and, therefore, disagreeable as it may be, this cannot be disregarded." And then the brief goes on to quote Richard Butler. And just to save a little bit of time, it's the Miletic brief at page 156. I'm not going to read the whole section that they quote. Suffice it to say that in the middle of their quote, there is a bracket and some ellipses, and what's left out of Butler's answer is, and I quote: "Not to mention the fact that given the context of the conflict to date, they probably wouldn't have a whole lot of confidence that they would be permitted to remain there anyway." It's the Prosecution's submission that that missing piece of testimony completely changes the nature of Butler's answer on that point and makes it useless for the Miletic brief to cite. He's standing for an entirely opposite proposition. You also heard testimony about, you may recall, General Simic, for example, talking about how the VRS was so sincere about the de-militarisation and cessation of hostility agreements in 1993 and again in 1995, and you were shown VRS documents ordering compliance, and then you were also shown documents showing the Muslim Army immediately ordering noncompliance. And I came across a document, and I just want to hit on it very briefly just to place things in a slightly more accurate context. I just point your attention to 5D01325, page 6 of the document, the English translation. This document is a transmission of an order from General Mladic to comply with the recent cessation of hostilities agreement in January of 1995. And General Simic notes in his order, following on that order: "Discuss with brigade commanders what should be done on the ground prior to the regional commission's arrival." And then in parentheses: "(Deployment and consolidation of combat security in some of the gaps, continuing fortification along the front and in the rear," and this is underlined, "and removal of weapons before inventory and removal by UNPROFOR)." And I don't want to hit that too hard, but I just want to kind of straighten out the historical record a little bit, because we did hear a lot of testimony about how sincere one side was, and I just didn't want to leave the mis-impression that based on the documents that are in evidence, and just bring that to your attention. I think it has been to be proven beyond any doubt that 155 was a telephone number. At page 231, paragraph 536, the Miletic brief disagrees, but you will recall the testimony over and over again about how that number connected to the numerous offices around the ops centre, General Milovanovic had it ring in his restroom -- or resting room, I should say, it was in one of the main ops rooms and so on and so forth. Take a look at P03176. It's the VRS Main Staff phone book. You'll see "155." Velo Pajic talked about that number at transcript page 28774. And the brief again quotes Richard Butler, but I'm afraid leaves out a very critical part of his testimony. And I'll just give you the page cites. You can go look -- look up and compare what's in the brief, what's not in the brief, what's clearly in the transcript, where Butler basically says, Yes, you're confronting me with what I testified to in Krstic. I thought 155 was a three-digit code, but I've learned a lot more since then. That's the great thing about this job. You learn something new every day. Clearly, my knowledge has expanded since I testified in Krstic. That's all left out. That's at transcript page 20607 to 20608. The brief -- the Miletic brief also concedes that the Main Staff was actively involved in the Drina Corps's activities concerning the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves in May of 1995. You may recall orders by General Krstic in mid-May of 1995 for the stabilisation of certain lines, directing certain assets to be moved here and there. Richard Butler testified about that. And what the Miletic brief does is, frankly, concedes that the Main Staff was on top of this activity, and it had to be. If you look at the orders, they deal with the 65th Protection Regiment, the 67th Communications. We have orders coming out of General Miletic's ops organ concerning these movements of troops, and again you'll recall the testimony that this was all part and parcel of what was going to happen in July. Your Honours, if I may, I think we're coming up shortly -- this is a good time for me to move on to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I want to look at paragraph 496 of the Miletic brief, page 215, where it states that: "When General Miletic went to Belgrade on 7 July 1995, the most he could have known was that the Drina Corps was to separate the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, that separation which didn't involve taking the enclaves, didn't involve deporting the population, General Miletic could, therefore, not have known the Muslim population would take refuge en masse in Potocari. Since he could not have known that the Muslim population was going to take refuge in Potocari, he could not have known that various criminal acts would take place." Obviously, from our position during trial and in our brief, we're not contesting in any real way General Miletic's quasi-alibi of being in Belgrade from the 7th through the 11th. Let's assume that it's been proven, just for the sake of argument. When General Miletic left for Belgrade, this is what he knew: He knew that the VRS had Zeleni Jadar by blasting the Dutch out of it on June 3rd, taking over that OP Echo. He knew that Krivaja 95 was underway. He knew that the Krivaja 95 attack plan called for splitting and shrinking the enclaves, which would recreate the humanitarian disaster which he all too well knew, and that that in turn, would create the conditions for the elimination of the enclaves, which is explicitly called for in that Krivaja 95 plan. He knew, when he left for Belgrade, that Krivaja 95, by its own words, was planned to implement Directives 7 and 7(1), both of which he drafted. He knew DutchBat was weakened. He knew the population was starving and miserable. That's what he knew before he even left. And let's assume, again for the sake of argument, Your Honours, that General Miletic had no contact whatsoever with the command post while he's on leave from 7 to 11 July. And I think everything that we have come to know about General Miletic, his work ethic, dedication to his job, to his function, to the war effort, and with the communications that were available by the Defence case's own testimony between the command post and Belgrade, tells us that, of course, General Miletic remained in contact with the command post when he was on leave. But in any event, for the sake of argument, what's the first thing that's going to happen when he gets back to the command post on 11 July? He's going to report to the most senior general there, and that's General Gvero, just like General Milovanovic did when he returned on the 19th, and he is duty-bound to receive a full report. If he hasn't heard already from watching the news, he's going to hear about Mladic being in Srebrenica, the Serbian flag on the church, and he's going to know that they've got this massive operation underway, monumental mobilisation of resources; buses, trucks, and fuel, one of the most strategic of all assets. Of course, he's going to know about these kinds of demands. The Miletic brief, at page 211, paragraph 489, asserts that: "While General Mladic deployed officers in Potocari, including some who belonged to the Main Staff, General Miletic was in Crna Rijeka and was carrying out his usual work without being involved in the events in Srebrenica and/or in Potocari." The Prosecution's position, the evidence has shown, that General Miletic could not properly be doing his job and not be involved and knowledgeable of those unfolding situations and the incredible demands that were being placed on the resources of the VRS during that period of time. Of course he's receiving information, and of course he's forwarding that to President Karadzic. And remember what Colonel Turkalj said. He, at least, always expected that President Karadzic would read those reports. These were important documents containing important information. And on the subject of fuel, I want to note at page 137, paragraph 315, the brief for Miletic makes the assertion that UNPROFOR, in fact, had 30.000 litres of fuel on its own premises during this operation, and cites the testimony of Colonel Trisic of the Bratunac Brigade. That ignores completely Colonel Franken's testimony at transcript 2492 to 2493 and at 2568 to 2570, on cross-examination, I add, that the VRS advanced the fuel for the transportations to the UN, because as the evidence has overwhelmingly established, the Dutch didn't have 30.000 litres of fuel at their disposal. You have to ignore a mountain of compelling testimony to come to the conclusion that DutchBat was sitting on that much fuel at that time. Lastly, I want to address the Miletic brief's discussion of the "full steam ahead" intercept, and this is at page 245, paragraph 569. The brief basically makes the argument that the Zepa plan had been made in Bratunac on the 12th, so it doesn't make sense that General Miletic has any knowledge that's going to help anybody at the time this conversation is held. I just want to point out, the simple fact is the situation on the ground was materially different on the 17th of July than it was on the 12th. I can't make it any more simple than that. It wasn't the 12th of July anymore. They had encountered fierce fighting. The reality on the ground, as General Miletic knew, had changed significantly in those five days. Your Honours, the Prosecution is not asking you to convict General Miletic for being the chief of Operations and Training Administration or standing in for the chief of staff or being the deputy chief of staff. We are asking you to convict General Miletic because he knowingly participated in that common plan to forcibly remove the Muslim populations from Srebrenica and Zepa. Whether you refer to him as the soul of the army, the nerve centre, the hub, the evidence has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that General Radivoje Miletic remained and chose to remain at the heart of that JCE, that joint criminal enterprise, to relentlessly seek to remove the Muslim population from the eastern enclaves, and the evidence has shown that he made significant contributions to do so. We ask you to return a guilty verdict for all the crimes with which General Miletic has been charged. Now, I want to turn to General Gvero. And again along the lines of this sort of responding rather than reiterating, I want to clarify a couple of mis-statements which I think require addressing. The brief contends that there is no evidence that General Gvero met Mladic in 1991 -- pardon me. The brief contends that the first time General Mladic and General Gvero met was in 1991. There's no evidence of that. That's unadorned by any fact or evidence. Page 109, paragraph 38, there's no evidence of the alleged discussions contained in there, as far as I can see. In addition, there are various citations to General Gvero's own statement, which is fine, except they don't support the assertions set forth in the brief. So, again, there's facts which are being alleged which have no evidential foundation in this record. I want to turn to two meetings which the brief discusses and just try to correct a little erroneous citation; paragraph 110 -- page 110, paragraph 39. These are two reports having to do with meetings between General Smith and various VRS officers on 22 and 25 August 1995; Exhibit numbers P02949 and P02950 respectively. With respect to the 22 August meeting, the Gvero brief suggests that General Gvero was not invited. However, there is no evidence that he was not invited. There is just no record that he was there. In fact, the report of the meeting makes it clear that only local VRS officers attended that meeting with Mladic and that there was no other VRS general there. With respect to the 25 August meeting, the report of the meeting makes it clear that General Mladic was not accompanied by all his commanders, as the brief states. Rather, it's just Generals Gvero and Tolimir getting down to business with General Smith and General Mladic, as the report records. On page 226, paragraph 329, there's a citation to a newspaper article. As far as I know, that's never been shown, it's never been on any exhibit list. It appears for the first time in a Defence brief. I stand to be corrected, but I just urge the Court to give it the evidential value that that deserves. The brief also, I believe, selectively quotes from General Milovanovic's testimony, and this is in the brief at paragraphs 1 -- paragraph 135, footnote 291. It suggests that General Gvero was not a member of the inner collegium, but ignores General Milovanovic's [Realtime transcript read in error "General Gvero"] testimony that Mladic would attend with "all his assistants." I want to turn for a few moments to the briefs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript, line 15 and 14, I think that needs to be corrected. "But ignores" not General Gvero's testimony, but Milovanovic's testimony. And then if I heard you correctly, you added that General Mladic would return with all his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I misspoke, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you did not misspeak. It's the transcript which is not correct. I mean, it's -- that's what you said. You referred to Milovanovic's testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to the effect that according to him, General Mladic always would return with all his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That the meetings would be attended by all his assistants, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to the brief's treatment of Colonel Kingori. You saw Colonel Kingori first on the trial video. You saw him out and about on the 12th, on the 13th, in Potocari, making himself useful, pushing, asking the questions, raising the issues that somebody needed to raise. What's going on over there at that house? That's no good. The person you see doing that is Colonel Kingori. Even in the new Potocari video that we just came into possession of, if you watch closely and you see that bread being distributed on the 12th, in addition to Colonel Popovic for a while, you see Joseph Kingori. You've heard those UNMO reports, Your Honours, written in the midst of that horror, which he experienced from Srebrenica, along that flow of terrified refugees up to Srebrenica, and then during that period of two days. His courage was challenged with anonymous snippets from the Niod report, yet I had to show him the material which spoke to his courage and the accuracy of his recollection. Is anybody really suggesting that Joseph Kingori was counting those shells, that Colonel Franken didn't tell his soldiers to stop counting because it had gotten over 150, or 200, or whatever it was? Is anybody really suggesting that Joseph Kingori did not see and did not hear and did not accurately report what's in those contemporaneous, desperate, horrified, and ultimately tragic reports, talking about tears being in their eyes? The shelling argument in the Gvero brief, at page 152, paragraph 173, and then at page 153, footnote 65, sets out a portion of the testimony you would have to ignore of the shelling. And it's set forth in our brief, paragraph 283, footnote 666 to 668. Joseph Kingori left this courtroom telling you -- giving you just a sense of what happened there. Now, on the same topic of shelling, I just want to point out that the Gvero brief at pages 163 to 164, paragraph 197, simply ignores Lieutenant Egbers' testimony that he was, in fact, trapped by the shelling, that when he moved from one point to the other he was followed. Now, let me turn to General Gvero's threats and his pressure on Generals Nicolai and Gobillard. Let there be no mistake about it. General Nicolai remained firm that it was his conversation on 11 July, 1610 hours, with General Gvero, combined with the other threats that DutchBat was receiving, which led the United Nations to discontinue its air support that day. Of course General Gvero knew about those other threats. He had to know. Of course he knew that DutchBat was being targeted; and I won't repeat the arguments in our brief. 6D00207, Gvero's warning to the Drina Corps to treat UNPROFOR decently, touted by the Defence, speaks to the opposite. It speaks to his recognition that what he was telling the public and telling UNPROFOR were lies. And I'll spare you the quote from that exhibit, but it's not intended to be a humanitarian gesture towards UNPROFOR, as the document itself states. There are multifarious purposes for treating them that way. Now, Colonel Fortin might have testified that the decision had been made to end the air-strikes by the time General Gvero and General Gobillard spoke, but General Gvero didn't know that, and that's why he starts off that conversation acknowledging in the conversation that General Gobillard still has close air support available to him at any time. And General Gvero repeats that the decision to use close air support was irrational, and he tones down his threat just a little bit, but his intention is clear. He wants to keep those aeroplanes out of the air. He doesn't know if the UN is going to put them back up there. So when he speaks to Gobillard again, he stresses again and again that the air support not be continued, and he says, If UN soldiers do not take any actions today, they will be safe. And he characterises the prior day's air support as a fatal mistake. And it's important to note that Fortin did not have the impression, during this conversation, that General Gvero was side-lined or marginalised in any respect, and I think the evidence has been proven conclusively that this idea that General Gvero was somehow put out to pasture or stuck in a corner somewhere in 1995 simply holds no water. Your Honours, there can be no reasonable doubt that Gvero's threat prompted Generals Gvero and Gobillard to decide to suspend the use of NATO air power to stop the Serb advance on Potocari. When you have the most senior VRS officer, General Gvero, making a statement like that to General Nicolai on 11 July during that 1610 conversation, it must be taken seriously, and he knows it's going to be taken seriously, and it was. There is no question that that conversation and General Gvero's threats contributed significantly to General Nicolai and General Gobillard's decision to suspend the air support. And what we have in the brief to impeach General Nicolai, I'm afraid, is an absolutely baseless personal attack on him. At page 120, paragraph 8, I quote: "Like many in UNPROFOR, perhaps for sound reasons, but that is not the issue in this trial, he," meaning General Nicolai, "was not keen on the Bosnian Serbs in general, and in its senior military leadership in particular." There is no evidence in this record of any partiality or prejudice on the behalf of General Nicolai, none, other than the words of counsel suggesting it, yet the brief persists in peddling that at page 180, paragraph 232. That Nicolai claimed that he was not personally under pressure during this period, I think we can attribute to a general's pride and nothing more, but the evidence has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the pressure exerted on him and General Gobillard during those conversations with General Gvero was obvious and enormous, and was a significant contribution to the JCE to remove the Muslim population. The Gvero brief also challenges the intercept of General Gvero and President Karadzic. There are two intercepts which follow General Gvero's conversation with General Nicolai, which you may recall, and in their brief the Gvero Defence spends some time challenging PW-145, trying to impeach his factual knowledge of certain things, calling him conceded. PW-145 clearly testified that his understanding was that General Gvero, on the 11th of July, was the only senior officer at the Main Staff. The intercept contains the phrase "at the Supreme Command." PW-145 testified he wasn't sure what the difference was. Whether he knew the difference between the Supreme Command or the Main Staff, Pale or Crna Rijeka, he knew that it was the VRS headquarters, and that's what was important, and he was right. The Defence brief accuses him of being conceded for testifying that they didn't write anything down that they weren't sure of, and I won't belabour the intercept heaven we were in for who knows how many months where operator after operator told you, It did us no good to write down something that we couldn't verify six ways to Sunday. If we didn't know something, we wouldn't put it down, or we'd indicate that we didn't know with a question mark. What he testified clearly was the way he identified President Karadzic as being the other participant; must have been, as you've heard time and time again, there was a subordinate connecting the call, holding. Often times, they would hear that connection being made, and somebody would say, Hold for the president, Hold for President Karadzic, Hold for General Mladic, whomever. The evidence has been proven beyond a reasonable doubt, through our intercept testimony, that that method worked and it worked well. The references in the Gvero brief at pages 197 and 201 are not helpful. They try to impeach PW-145's conclusion that he was listening to a conversation between General Gvero and President Karadzic by comparing the transcript of that conversation to a transcript of the tape. We have an audiotape of this conversation. And the big point the brief makes is, See, on the tape transcript there's no identification of Karadzic as being the caller or the participant, and there's only X and Y listed. There's none of this other extraneous information that PW-145 mistakenly put in there. The problem is that transcript is created by the OTP, by one of our language assistants, listening to the tape, so it's not evidence of anything. It's not a MUP or an ABiH document; it's just our document. And I invite Your Honours to look at the comparative intercepts that the Defence has proffered to you in their attempt to suggest that Gvero, in this conversation, was actually speaking to somebody else to whom he was referring as "President." They use as an example a conversation he has with Professor Koljevic, whom he refers to as, I believe, "Vice-President," "Professor" and "President." But please look carefully at these conversations. What you'll note, I think, is that these are friendly, conversational, small-talk in some places, conversations. The Defence would have you believe that the conversation at issue is too cordial to represent the actual fractured relationship between General Gvero and President Karadzic, but when you look at this intercept at issue, it is short, curt, polite as it should be, and no more, quite to the contrary of what the Defence would have you believe. It further establishes that this call is with President Karadzic and not somebody with whom he has a more friendly relationship, like Professor Koljevic, where you'll see again a much more conversational, talkative, and lengthy intercept. We've heard a lot of testimony about General Gvero's 13 July order to block the passage of the Muslim column. You heard a lot of witnesses try to minimise General Gvero's operational experience, his combat experience, and there's no evidence that when General Gvero issued that order that anyone anywhere said, Hang on, this is coming out from General Gvero, this is outside his corps competency. Why? He's only ever commanded a platoon. We can't follow this order. He's the morale guy. When that order went out, it was taken as seriously as its subject matter deserved. The Gvero brief would literally have you believe that General Gvero was treated something as a joke. General Nicolai wasn't laughing, General Gobillard wasn't laughing, and General Zivanovic was not laughing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Thayer. And sorry for the interruption, but we have a small technical problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. President. When General Zivanovic received that order, he did not hesitate to implement it, to pass it on virtually verbatim. And there is nothing unusual about this order going out under General Gvero's name. General Mladic had to rely on his closest assistants to be able to execute these types of tasks for him. General Milovanovic couldn't do it all by himself, particularly when he wasn't at the command post. And time and time again, we see the assistant commanders, take Tolimir, for example, acting putatively outside their corps competencies, providing combat proposals. Take a look at P00187, 13 July, Tolimir doing just that, offering combat proposals; P02794, 21 July, the infamous chemical weapons document. It would be more propitious if we bombed the columns of refugees. But in addition to that, you'll see he provides other combat advice. And even the Miletic Defence concedes, at page 247, paragraph 574, that assistant commanders could be tasked outside their corps competencies. P000 -- one too many zeros, P00186, 29 July, Richard Butler testified another combat order by Tolimir. Again, it should come as no surprise that PW-168 testified that when he was given an order by General Miletic, he understood that General Miletic was giving him that order in the name of General Mladic. This is how this Main Staff operated. It was their job to give proposals, and sometimes it was their job to be tasked to do something that a general officer should be able to do by virtue of the fact that he is a general officer. I want to address very briefly the Boksanica video. I'm not going to belabour the back-and-forthing on that. It's all in the brief. We're taken to task in the Gvero brief for our cross-examination, or lack thereof, of certain of those witnesses. With a lot of the testimony, it's not inconsistent with what our theory is, that he was there both days, number one. Number two, the proposition that's being proffered, that General Gvero was there only because he couldn't personally communicate with General Mladic to tell him about the extreme situation in the Krajina is preposterous. We know that General Gvero was with General Mladic on the 25th at a meeting with General Smith. You've seen the video yourselves, Your Honours. General Gvero is peeling a label off a beer bottle, chatting up Simun Dudnjik, the Ukrainian commander, talking to Hamdija Torlak, having a jolly time with Vinko Pandurevic, General Krstic, and General Mladic is there the entire time. And you heard some testimony during the trial about what's been described as a fractious relationship between Generals Gvero and Mladic. You heard that they fight. You heard that General Gvero disagreed with General Mladic. You even heard from one witness that General Mladic basically ignored anything that General Gvero said. I think the evidence in this case is overwhelmingly to the contrary. And I'll just throw out some exhibit numbers, Your Honours, to take a look at. P04036, just a routine convoy request from UNPROFOR, helicopter flights, that General Mladic writes in three places on three pages, Toso, Gvero, your proposals, your attitude, actively obviously seeking their input as his trusted assistants. P02757, General Gvero's letter to General Karadzic, stating in no uncertain terms who he understands his superior to be and whose orders he singularly followed during the war; Ratko Mladic. P03938, General Mladic's appraisal of General Gvero, dated October 1995. Admittedly, he's reviewing a period of General Gvero's work that lasts through 1994, based on his reference to the Lukavac 93 operation which the evidence shows involved the liberation of Trnovo in 1994. He can't explain why that document is dated 1995, but it's got a different performance appraisal date. He simply can't explain it, don't know why. General Gvero clearly had the ability to disagree with General Mladic, but he could do that and keep his job, I think the evidence in this case has shown, is based on the anecdotal evidence of General Mladic and his personality. That wouldn't happen if he didn't trust and value that person. We see Gvero and Mladic side by side again and again; meetings with Smith in April, going to see President Karadzic with Mladic June 1, July and August meeting with Mladic and Smith. Is there any doubt in anyone's mind that if General Mladic for a minute thought that General Gvero wasn't significantly contributing to that war effort, he would have been gone? This evidence that you've heard from time to time about disagreements, even fighting, that's evidence of their closeness, Your Honours. It's the people with whom we are most intimate and trusted with whom we can be the most frank. General Milovanovic specifically rejected Defence counsel's proposition that General Gvero had no influence on command, and that's at transcript page 12249. And we see that when Mladic needs to do business, when he's meeting with the Smiths, the Akashis, the Karadzics, he brings Gvero, he brings Tolimir, his close assistants. The Gvero brief makes a number of assertions about General Gvero that I want to respond to. It refers to the entire philosophy of the VRS Morale Sector which strove for specialist qualifications, good discipline, strict adherence to the rules of engagement, and respect for human rights, was ridiculed, and this diminished the authority of the sector, in general, and of Milan Gvero in particular. It refers to General Gvero's deeply-felt commitment to justice, discipline, and good order. It claims that Milan Gvero was renowned to have been the only good man on the Main Staff. And you even read in the brief that General Gvero never heard about the crimes, even after they were committed. That's at page 118, paragraph 3. I want to recall for you, Your Honours, P01334A. It's a 25 July 1995 intercept at 0950. General Gvero is speaking with a friend by the name of Subara, and Subara tells Gvero: "I'm calling to tell you to watch out what you're doing over there in Zepa, not to let it be like in Srebrenica, because there is talk that they slaughtered and rampaged there." And what is General Gvero's response: "They're lying, man, they're lying." Ever the propagandist, he lies even to this friend, who again says later in the conversation, and I quote: "Yes, that's smart, because they criticised us badly for Srebrenica." General Gvero, obviously up to date on what's happening in Zepa, tells him how exactly they're going to undertake the transportations of the civilians out of the enclave, and his friend to that says: "Yes, that's smart, because they criticised us badly for Srebrenica." And Gvero's response, and I quote: "They're just making things up. What else can they do? There's nothing else they can do but lie." Your Honours, General Gvero stood up before you, and he had his chance to express some genuine remorse for these horrendous crimes. Did he even acknowledge that a crime had been committed against the Muslim populations of Srebrenica or Zepa? He said something to the effect, Any loss of life is tragic. And then he couldn't help himself and immediately said, But to talk about one side and not the other, that doesn't help matters. When he spoke to you, Your Honours, he couldn't even say the words "Srebrenica" or "Zepa." His contributions to the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove the Muslim populations from Srebrenica and Zepa were numerous and they were significant, and we ask that you find him guilty of the crimes with which he has been charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Vanderpuye is now in the courtroom. I take it that you are going next. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. It is my privilege to appear before you today, Your Honours, to deliver the closing arguments on behalf of the Prosecution concerning the accused Ljubisa Beara and Vujadin Popovic. I will endeavour to limit my submissions to the evidence that directly links these accused to the crimes with which they have been charged under the indictment. And except to briefly underscore and highlight some of the overwhelming evidence against Mr. Beara and Mr. Popovic, as I will address each in turn, I will try, to the greatest extent possible, to avoid restating the arguments that are already set out in the Prosecution's extensive trial brief. Between Mr. Beara and Mr. Popovic, they have challenged almost every aspect of the indictment, including aspects of the crime base itself, ranging from the number of dead to their identity as Muslims. In the case of Mr. Beara, besides basically acknowledging his position as chief of security of the Main Staff of the VRS, the Defence essentially denies the entire case against the accused, and Mr. Popovic is only slightly less contentious. They have every right to do so, and it is our burden, clearly, to prove the charges in the indictment beyond a reasonable doubt, and we accept that burden, Your Honours, and we're confident that the evidence in this case absolutely proves the guilt of Mr. Beara and Mr. Popovic of the charged offences beyond any reasonable doubt. The Beara Defence brief, at paragraph 42, basically states that the Prosecution has, among other things, manipulated facts out of context in the presentation of this case. And while levelling these types of allegations in its final submissions is, in my view, of questionable value, I just want to reiterate a couple of things: First, that we fully rely and we stand on the record of these proceedings. We're entirely confident that the Trial Chamber -- in the Trial Chamber's ability to independently review, scrutinise, and to fairly deliberate and consider the established facts just as they are in the record, and we have full confidence in the strength of the case that has been presented against these accused. The facts establishing Mr. Beara and, for that matter, Mr. Popovic's culpability and that warrant their conviction of the charged offences in this case speak loudly and they speak clearly. Most importantly, Your Honours, they speak for themselves. The Defence brief, that is, Mr. Beara's brief, is replete with arguments to the effect that Beara did not know and was not aware of the crimes that were being perpetrated. I'm quoting from paragraph 494. And this is predicated predominantly on two defences, and they are related. One is an alibi defence. As you are aware, Mr. Beara asserts that he was in Belgrade between 13-16 July 1995. And the second is what I would call an ID defence, and that is that he asserts that the identification evidence in this case against him is unproven because it is unreliable or even contrived. It seems to suggest that he may have been framed. The alibi defence that's put forward in Mr. Beara's direct case fails, and it fails for two fundamental reasons, Your Honours. First, it is intrinsically unreliable and it is incredible. The second is that even if it were not so, the evidence in this case, the intercept evidence, the documentary evidence, the eye-witness evidence, all considered together categorically disproves the alibi and establishes Mr. Beara's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. As you know, the Beara Defence called three alibi witnesses for this period. They called Mira Cekic, who was a friend of the Beara family, Svetlana Gavrilovic, also a friend of the family, and Milan Kerkes, a friend of Mr. Beara's son, Branko Beara, and they had been friends since the seventh grade before he testified. The Trial Chamber obviously had an opportunity to see and to hear each of these witnesses attest to their respective recollections and their knowledge of the events to which they testified. I won't go through the alibi extensively because it is, albeit, limitedly covered in the Prosecution's brief, but there are some points in that alibi testimony that I would like to highlight for the Trial Chamber because I think it is underscores just how utterly unbelievable and untenable that alibi defence really was. Svetlana Gavrilovic testified that she met Mr. Beara and his wife at the home of Mayor Cekic on the 14th of July. She claimed, among other things, that she could remember details, if you recall, from a 1993 birthday party for Mr. Beara, some 15 years before she actually testified in this case.
