And she testified without any priming, without anything to jog her memory, without any prompting, or, frankly, without any real good reason for her to be able to recall the details that she related to this Trial Chamber, but she testified in a feat that can only be considered unbelievable and really astonishing. She was able to recall from this 1993 birthday party how Mr. Beara was dressed. She testified that he had a T-shirt on, that it was a white T-shirt, that it had a logo on it, that it was a crew-neck and not a V-neck T-shirt. She testified that he had on casual pants, that they were either jeans or some other kind of pants. She even testified to what he was wearing on his feet. She testified that he had slippers on. And, oh, yes, she was able to tell us what colour they were. She said that they were dark blue. She remembered that from 1993. Then she testified about a 1995 birthday party, and she talked -- she gave the same level of detail with respect to the 1995 birthday party as well. She was able to tell us on that occasion what kind of shoes he was wearing or what colour shoes he was wearing, and told us that they were black shoes on that occasion, in addition to the other details concerning the alibi. She told you about the time that Mr. Beara came over to her place to fix her iron, and she remembered what he had on then also. On that occasion, he came, and she said that he was wearing a navy coat. He took off the coat and, oh, yes, she could remember what he was wearing under the coat, and on that occasion he had on a shirt with a sweater, and she could remember that. When it came to the more recent events, such as when it was that she actually met with the Defence investigator, Mr. Stanic, concerning her testimony, she gave the following answers to the following questions, if I could just read that in, and that's at transcript 24781, it's lines 9 through 20. The question is put to her by Mr. McCloskey: "Q. So a couple of months ago, maybe March or April, Mr. Stanic comes up to you and asks you about this important topic. You know that Mr. Beara is in The Hague. You know about genocide and mass murder, but you cannot tell me the date of this, the date he contacted you, Mr. Stanic, you can't even tell me the month?" "A. No, I can't, I really can't." When she's pressed, she says: "A. No, I can't, I can't give you the date. I can't remember. I don't know the date. "Q. Do you know the month? "A. Well, it may have been April, in the month of April, March or April when I met Mr. Stanic, thereabouts. "Q. What day? "A. I don't know, I really don't know. I did not consider this date worth retaining, remembering at all." That's about the only believable thing that she said during the course of her testimony. Why would anybody remember the level of details that she testified concerning what Mr. Beara wore in 1993 or what he wore in 1995 or what he wore when he came to fix her iron? Why would anybody consider that worth retaining? The fact is really nobody would. She made it up because she knew that it couldn't be checked. She made it up because she knew that it couldn't be verified. And the one thing that she wasn't sure that could be verified, she had no recollection of, and it was the most recent event, relative to Mr. Beara, prior to her testimony. The Trial Chamber should reject this testimony. It is not worthy of your consideration in respect of evaluating the charges against Mr. Beara. Milan Kerkes testified, and there was a young man who was a good friend of Mr. Beara's son, he was working, he was charming, and he actually seemed that he was being genuine with the Trial Chamber when he testified. And he testified about his trip to Montenegro with his friends, and he showed photographs, and he talked about how his friends had a good time and they were chasing girls, I think. He's testified that he went to the Beara home on 14 July. He saw Mr. Beara there. Branko told him that it was Mr. Beara's birthday, and according to Mr. Kerkes, they ended up leaving the next day. He said they took a bus and went down to Petrovac. Of course, there are infirmities in his story as well. You may recall that Mr. Kerkes testified that he came back from Petrovac after exactly two weeks. He said it was a Saturday, exactly two weeks. That's in the transcript at 24941, 23 through 24. And he said he wanted to come back to have a rest and start his practice the next day, Monday. He later said, and I just want to read from the transcript - this is at transcript page 24955 through 24956: "Q. All right. When you got back from your vacation, you went to your training, you said, right; that is, handball training? "A. We arrived at the weekend. I took a day rest, and then my coach, Pera Lazarevic, an Olympian, had the same system. He started preparations on the 1st of September. Since the 1st of September was a weekend, we started on Monday. There was a competition to be held soon, and we started our preparations on the first Monday after the 1st of September. "Q. Okay. Did you tell Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Stanic that your coaches name was Pera Lazarevic; did you tell them that? "A. I did. "Q. And you told them that you started on the 1st of September your training? You told them that too? "A. The 1st of August. "Q. The 1st of August? "A. Yes, I did." It sounded reasonable, it sounded confident. In fact, it was incorrect and it was a deceit. The 1st of August, as he corrected it, did not fall on a weekend, as he said. It did not fall on a Saturday, it did not fall on a Sunday, and, for that matter, it didn't fall on a Monday, either. The 1st of August fell exactly three weeks after the fall of Srebrenica, the 11th of July. That was a Tuesday. Why is this significant? It's significant because Mr. Kerkes' story about when it is that he got back and what it is he did in order to anchor the time that he was gone was related to the time that his practice started. He told us that his practice started on a Monday because the 1st of the month - he said September, but I think he meant August - fell on a weekend. It didn't. And if he started his practice the first Monday after the 1st of August, that was the 7th of August. And if that's when he started his practice, then he couldn't have left when he said he left. And if he did leave when he said he left, then he's got his times completely screwed up and he's an unreliable witness in terms of establishing the alibi that's been proffered by the Defence in this case. It's not just that he's wrong about the date, Your Honours. It's that he's wrong about the entire story that relates to the date. He gave an actual explanation as to why it is he knew that it was that Monday. He knew that it was Monday because the 1st was on the weekend, and in fact it wasn't. So the whole recollection and the basis of his recollection is contrived. Ironically, Mr. Kerkes said that he believed that he was interviewed by the Defence investigator in this case because, among his friends, he best recalled the events concerning the vacation, if you can recall that. In fact, he couldn't remember the name of the -- the address of the place that they stayed. By the time he testified in this case, he had already been there three times. He'd been there twice -- he'd been there once before in 1995, then again in 1995, according to his testimony, and then again in 1996. And when he testified here, he couldn't remember the address of the place. He couldn't remember the name of the street that it was on. He couldn't remember the name of the proprietor or the person through whom he made the booking in this case. He couldn't remember the date or the day of the week that Mr. Stanic called him to meet prior to his testimony. But he claimed that he could remember the circumstances surrounding their vacation better than Branko Beara, and you'll remember the reason why Branko Beara, according to Mr. Kerkes, was able to go on this vacation, to begin with, was because his father came home for his birthday and his father gave him some money, and that's how it was able to occur. Branko Beara's ability to go on this vacation with his friend, according to Kerkes, was entirely linked and connected to his father's birthday. I just want to read to you from the transcript a little bit, and this is on transcript 24946, pages [sic] 8 through 20. I'm sorry, lines 8 through 20. "Q. Well, you talked to him about this vacation; right? "A. With Branko? "Q. Yes. "A. As I said, from time to time, we go back to that vacation, but after I spoke with the attorney we didn't discuss that particularly. For some reason -- for some reason of his, he noticed that I can recall many details. He probably gave my phone number to the attorney and, in turn, he called me. "Q. Having discussed this with him, what kinds of details do you remember that he doesn't? "A. For example, the date when we left. He couldn't recall that. "Q. He doesn't remember the date that you left? "A. He doesn't." I'm sure you remember, as I've described, this whole story about how it is that Branko was able to go, and they discussed this trip not long before Mr. Kerkes testified. Kerkes immediately realised how implausible this had to be, because if the only reason that Branko Beara was able to go on this vacation was because his father was home to give him money, and they discussed this only a couple of months before he testified, it is inconceivable that he wouldn't remember how it is that he ended up going on that vacation, and that answer would make no sense whatsoever. It would undermine completely his testimony and undermine completely the accuracy with which he -- with which he purported to give it. So what did he do? He changed his answer right on the spot, and I know that that wasn't lost on the Trial Chamber. The Beara Defence has also advanced the proposition that the alibi is corroborated by entries in Bob Djordjevic's diary concerning Milos Tomovic, a posit that it is logical to conclude that Tomovic would have driven Beara to Belgrade on that morning when he was stopped together with Djordjevic on 13 July by military police. Now, I don't know about the logic of making that conclusion, but I don't see that there's evidence in the record that Tomovic drove Mr. Beara to Belgrade. There's just no hard evidence of that in the record. I would submit to the Trial Chamber, as I said, that the alibi evidence presented as to Mr. Beara fails because it is not reliable, it fails because it's not credible, and, most importantly, it fails because it simply does not reflect the truth about where Mr. Beara was and what he was doing between 13 and 16 July 1995. The Beara Defence also posits a notion of an unreliable identification in the alternative. In their brief, the Defence argue that the identification evidence against Mr. Beara is the product of either erroneous processes or factors which have tainted its accuracy and reliability. They also argue that certain identifying witnesses deliberately mis-identified or implicated Mr. Beara in order to serve their own ulterior motives and to diminish their own criminal responsibility in this case. According to paragraphs 43 and 133 through 137 of the Defence brief, these witnesses "mis-characterised, distorted and manipulated the evidence to avoid indictment." In short, the suggestion is that Mr. Beara was scapegoated or even framed in respect of the charges levelled against him in this case. Some 14 witnesses identified Mr. Beara in and around the Zvornik and Bratunac areas and Nova Kasaba during the period that was claimed by his -- in his alibi. Over the period of 13 and 14 July, about ten witnesses identify him. This evidence cannot be compartmentalised or viewed in insular or disjointed fragments. It really has to be viewed in the context of the whole. It has to be viewed in light of the other evidence in this case. And viewed in this light, the truth about Mr. Beara's whereabouts during the critical periods set out in the indictment is plain, and it's evident in the trial record. That evidence is found in the documentary evidence in this case, the intercept evidence in this case, and, of course, the testimonial record. And you've heard and you've seen these identifying witnesses, and you've had the opportunity to consider their evidence in light of all the other compelling evidence in this case. The Defence expert, Mr. Wagenaar, did not consider that other evidence, and the conclusions contained in his report, as well as in his testimony, painfully reflect that. You may recall that when he was confronted, he conceded that he did not review the statements of witnesses other than the 12 that were selected by the Defence. He did not realise that Mr. Beara had appeared on wanted posters in determining whether or not it was appropriate to place certain witnesses in a line-up. He obviously didn't consider that in suggesting the propriety of conducting these identification tests, either photo arrays or line-ups. You recall that he testified how he was unable to discover any photos where Mr. Beara was not wearing glasses, because it was relevant to a particular identification, and again affecting his judgement as to the propriety of implementing identification procedures. He was confronted with P03695, which was an internet print-out showing Mr. Beara without glasses in an image from 2004. The one thing he said that was significant and I submit that the Trial Chamber should countenance is that names are basically easier to remember than faces; you can refresh your recollection of a name by repeating a story much easier than you can a face. He noted that while it may be difficult at times to recall a face with respect to a name, there's no reason why the memory should fail. He indicated also that the same goes for someone who's familiar to the identifying party. And I just want to briefly remind the Court of who some of these identifying witnesses are and the context in which they identified and implicated Mr. Beara and these events. Zlatan Celanovic, is a Bratunac legal officer who, on 10 or 11 July, puts Beara in front of the Bratunac headquarters together with Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of the interpreters, who don't have the text you're reading out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the evening of 13 July, after 2100 hours sometime, Celanovic met Beara and discussed with him the large number of prisoners then in Bratunac. He was with Mr. Beara as he toured Bratunac, surveying the security situation concerning the Muslim men and boys who were held on buses throughout the town. Remarkably, while the Defence assert that this never happened, they also argue that it shows that Beara lacked genocidal intent because he talked about transferring prisoners to Kladanj. I don't think those two things can coexist. By the time Mr. Beara discussed transportation with Celanovic, he had already met Momir Nikolic at the centre of town and he had already ordered him to go and see Drago Nikolic of the Zvornik Brigade in order to provide him with details concerning the thousands of prisoners to be sent to Zvornik and to be killed there. Telling Celanovic the prisoners were going to Kladanj, rather than showing a lack of intent, shows cunning and shows manipulation. It's the same thing you see on a 13 July intercept, where it is claimed that Beara is sending transportation to take the prisoners to Batkovica. Beara never arranged or carried out any such transportation. It never happened. And what you have here is not evidence of -- that's exculpatory. You have evidence of a pretext, and what you have evidence of is intent. As the chief of security of the VRS Main Staff, it makes perfect sense that Mr. Beara met with Celanovic concerning the prisoners. Celanovic was directly involved in those matters, and indeed you may recall that he was involved with one particular prisoner, Resic Junanovic [phoen], who was the former head of the police station in Bratunac. And you know that Resic Junanovic, who was in the custody of the VRS, was never seen again. Celanovic knew Beara, he described him, and there is really no reasonable doubt as to the veracity of his testimony. PW-161 also was called over to the SDS offices in Bratunac on the evening of 13 July, and there Mr. Beara asked him about the availability of certain machinery and manpower. He told PW-161 that it was needed because there were a lot of dead that needed to be buried. When PW-161 later returned to the SDS offices that night, Mr. Beara directed him to go to a location where a grave was to be dug. And the next day, after some trouble getting the grave dug, he assured PW-161 that a backhoe excavator would be provided in order to assist in carrying out the job of burying the victims of the Kravica warehouse massacre. PW-162 met Mr. Beara on the morning of 14 July at the SDS offices at around 9.30 in the morning. Importantly, Mr. Beara introduced himself by name. Even according to the Defence witness, Mr. Wagenaar, there's no reason why his recollection of the name should fail. On that occasion, there were two other VRS officers with Mr. Beara who engaged PW-162 to obtain certain construction equipment from the brickworks factory, which included a loader. There is evidence in this case that even co-accused Ljubomir Borovcanin identified Mr. Beara. On 12 July or thereabouts, he indicated that he saw Mr. Beara with Miroslav Deronjic in the centre Bratunac discussing the Muslim column moving towards Zvornik. That's Exhibit P02852, pages 76 through 77. 13 July, he saw Mr. Beara at the Bratunac headquarters, arguing with Miroslav Deronjic sometime after 8.00 p.m. on 13 July. And according to Mr. Borovcanin, Beara was insistent that all the captured be brought to Bratunac, and Deronjic was adamantly against it. You have in the record the testimony of Mr. Deronjic, who says that on 13 July Mr. Beara tells him he's there to kill the prisoners, and on 14 July he goes to the Ciljani [phoen] brickworks factory, where he confronts Beara and tells him not to kill anybody. And this follows Mr. Beara's meeting with PW-162, where he is galvanising this engineering equipment and is told -- rather, the other officers are told that there may be equipment available for them at the brickworks factory. You have the testimony of Momir Nikolic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time it's convenient for you, it's break time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just about to segue. You have that testimony, that is, the testimony of Momir Nikolic. That you received recently, and I'm sure you recall it very well. And we're not asking you to make anything more out of this testimony than you can find is reasonably corroborated by the evidence in this case. I would submit, however, that there is plenty of corroboration. I think now we can break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Twenty-five minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There are just a few other witnesses I would like to cover. I'm not covering all of the ones that are in the brief, but I think they're important to highlight for the Trial Chamber. There was a witness at Nova Kasaba. It was a DutchBat, Vincent Egbers. He places Mr. Beara at Nova Kasaba on 14 July, and you can recall that he wrote down Beara's name as the person that he met in an entry that he placed in a contemporaneous report. That's 2D0024, it's on page 6, item 10, and it reads: "I gave an account of what happened to us, which was written down. Colonel Beara has the original, and there is a copy in the possession of Section 23." In Zvornik, there are also witnesses. There was Milorad Bircakovic, who placed Mr. Beara at the Zvornik Brigade on the morning of 14 July 1995; which is when he met with Drago Nikolic and Vujadin Popovic concerning the transfer of the prisoners that would be arriving shortly thereafter from Bratunac. The Beara Defence brief, at paragraph 175, states that: "Bircakovic never saw Ljubisa Beara," and I don't believe that's the case. The record states at transcript 11097, 4 through 8, Bircakovic said that when Popovic and Beara arrived, everyone saw it. And then at transcript 11102, 5 through 7, he states: "When I arrived, Popovic and Beara arrived as well, so they went into the barracks and I saw them go in." So I don't think there's any ambiguity on that point, but I thought I would bring that to the attention of the Trial Chamber. You'll recall, of course, that not long after that meeting, the prisoners are brought up from Bratunac by bus. On the 14 July, we also have an identification of Mr. Beara within a few metres of the Petkovci school, and that was by Marko Milosevic. On that occasion, he placed Mr. Beara at the school on the late afternoon of 14 July 1995, and you will recall that on that occasion it was Drago Nikolic who pointed out Mr. Beara to Mr. Milosevic; clearly, somebody who knows who Beara was on 14 July 1995. It was PW-104 who met with Mr. Beara on 14 July at the Zvornik Brigade and asked for assistance -- where he asked for assistance with burials. He said: "We have a lot of prisoners, and it's very hard for us to control them. They are at various locations in the Zvornik municipality. We have to get rid of them. I expect assistance from the municipality." PW-104, of course, understood that to mean burying the executed prisoners. PW-165 testified that he heard that Beara was at the Command of the Zvornik Brigade on 15 July 1995, when he saw Vujadin Popovic as well. He was told that the two were there to meet with the commander. On 16 July, we have an identification of Mr. Beara at the Kula school by Slavko Peric, and this is a little bit more interesting than the others. In this particular instance, Mr. Peric puts both Mr. Beara and Mr. Popovic at the Kula school at the time that the prisoners there are being loaded onto buses and driven a few kilometres away to the Branjevo Farm, where they were shot and executed. If I just could read a little bit from the transcript, this is at transcript page 11414, and I asked Mr. Peric: "Q. Did you ever reach a conclusion as to who those officers were, who they were that you saw on the 16th of July? "A. Well, approximately, they bore some similarity to those men that I described. "Q. And who were the people that you saw in the press? What were their names? "A. No, really, I wouldn't like to name anyone. "Q. Do you recall if you previously named anyone? "A. Yes, possibly. "Q. Who did you name? "A. I named Beara and Popovic." Now, it's clear from his answer that he was equivocating about the identification that he had previously given, but I would submit to Your Honours that the reason why he was equivocating about the prior identification is because the prior identification was a correct one. The prior identification was made at a time where he was not confronted with the accused sitting in a courtroom. He described both Mr. Beara and he described Mr. Popovic in the transcript. The only reason why he would not want to answer the question, if the prior identification he gave was merely an approximation, would be because it's accurate. It's the only reason why he wouldn't want to answer. And I would submit that that identification, particularly of Mr. Popovic, and I'll address that later, is corroborated by other evidence, such as intercept evidence, connecting him to the events in Pilica. As to Mr. Beara, it is simply just as strong evidence. The identification evidence that I've gone over, I hope, has highlighted the infirmity of the defence that has been put forward by the Beara Defence in terms of identification, the strength of identification, and, of course, alibi, and I would submit to the Trial Chamber that what we have here is a complete failure of the alibi and identification defences as advanced by the Beara team. Realistically, Your Honours, for those defences to work, given the diversity of the identifying witnesses, the corroborating documentary evidence, the corroborating intercept evidence, it would require the most elaborate, calculated, and coordinated plan among all of these witnesses, many of whom are unknown to each other, many of whom, in the case of intercept operators, are on the opposing side. It doesn't make sense. The alternative is that somebody's walking around confidently with a Beara suit on, impersonating the chief of security of the VRS, in the Main Staff of the VRS, to VRS officers in an area controlled by VRS, expecting not to get caught, expecting not to get in trouble, and expecting to get away with it. That's not a realistic or viable alternative to the strength of the identification evidence that's been adduced before this Trial Chamber. There is evidence of direct involvement -- of Mr. Beara's direct involvement in the crimes with which he's been charged, and that evidence you can find in the intercepts in this case. Now, the Defence refer to an intercept at 11.25 on 13 July. It's P1341. I had mentioned it earlier, but I think I'll mention it again. This is an intercept that states: "Colonel Ljubo is sending four buses, two trucks, one trailer to Kasaba to transport Muslim prisoners, and they will be dispatched to the camp in Batkovici village where they will be sorted into war criminals and normal soldiers." Now, the Beara Defence has put forward that this shows a lack of criminal intent, it's an entirely legitimate thing to do. I would submit to the Trial Chamber that it shows quite the opposite. But before I get there, I want to point out a couple things. One, it's not clear from the intercept who's actually speaking. It's not clear from the intercept what the source of the information is. It says Beara is going to do something, but it doesn't say who's reporting it, or where it's being reported from, or where the information is coming from. It doesn't show you anything about his intent, because you don't know who's conveying the information or where, in fact, it came from. The other thing is if it does come from Mr. Beara, then it calls into question his alibi defence, it calls into question his identification defence, and it calls into question the veracity of the Defence case, because it shows, Your Honours, that he's aware of the situation, he's aware of the prisoners in Kasaba, he's aware of how many, they are given the number of trucks and buses and such that would be sent there to pick them up, and he's involved with the disposition of those prisoners when he should be on his way home to celebrate his birthday. I would submit to you that what it shows is evidence of intent, because when you look at a different intercept, that's intercept P01130, this is the 10.09 intercept on 13 July, and this one was an intercept that was rather hotly contested by the Beara Defence, but this is an intercept which begins Beara speaking, and he speaks to "Senor Lucic." What he says to "Senor Lucic" is: "Did you hear me? Do you know the 400 balijas that have shown up in Konjevic Polje?" And Lucic says: "I know." And he says: "Where are they now," and the conversation continues. "Have they been disarmed, have they been rounded up?" And Beara says: "Excellent." Lucic says -- I'm sorry, Beara says -- Lucic says: "There's a huge group there." And Beara says: "Okay, well, you can also -- those 20," as written, it says on the intercept, "so the forces are not dispersed, shove them all in the playground. Who gives a fuck about them." Lucic says: "Okay." And Beara says: "They're locked up, right?" And he confirms that. Then he tells them to line them up in rows of four and five. I'm sure you remember this intercept. This was corroborated by an to aerial image showing the prisoners lined up in Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down for the benefit of the interpreters and the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could comply, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. Later on in this intercept, Mr. Beara gets connected to Zoka, Zoran Malinic. Malinic tells him during the course of this intercept that: "They're killing themselves. There are also plenty of wounded." And Mr. Beara says: "You mean they're doing it amongst themselves?" And Malinic repeats: "They're killing." And Beara says: "Well, excellent, just let them continue." In the light of this intercept, the following intercept, talking about sending buses - buses, by the way, that never arrived, never got to Batkovica - suggests that the 11.25 intercept, if it is Mr. Beara, is a pretext, and that makes it even worse because it shows conning and planning in order to manipulate unsuspecting people. Alternatively, it shows that somebody else made the call and the information may not be reliable, in which case it doesn't show any evidence of intent. It's certainly not exculpatory, as posited by the Defence in this case. Sorry, just bear with me for one moment. I wanted to show you another intercept which I think also speaks volumes about Mr. Beara's intent and his involvement in the charged JCEs in this case. This is an intercept that's P1179, and this is an intercept where Mr. Beara is speaking to General Krstic. And you may recall this is the intercept which begins that Furtula didn't carry out the boss's order. And in this intercept, Mr. Beara's seeking to obtain 30 men that were ordered on 15 July; it's at 10.00 a.m. He's going through the command structure in order to get the personnel or galvanise the personnel needed to carry out the orders with which he's been tasked, and we submit those orders are to carry out executions. He's not just walking in and taking people and ordering them around and usurping the command chain. What this intercept shows is that he's operating entirely within the command chain, and it's a fine example of exactly how the security organ functioned in relation to the command organ and to the command structure of the VRS. This intercept is significant because at the very end of it, you hear Mr. Beara say, after he tries to get these men -- General Krstic refers him to Indzic, and General Krstic refers him to Blagojevic, try to get the men from the MUP, and Mr. Beara says: "I don't know what to do. I mean, like, Krle, still -- there are still 3500 parcels that I have to distribute, and I have no solution." And General Krstic says: "I'll see what I can do." These 3500 parcels, the Defence has suggested, can't be properly defined or are insufficiently defined for the Trial Chamber to rely on, and I would submit that that term is very clear. Not only is it clear in this intercept, but it's clear in other intercepts as well. In their brief, the Defence cite -- I seem to have lost my place, but I believe they cite to Rakic, who defines this term as units, and in fact there is evidence in this case which more clearly defines it. The evidence in this case that defines it, and defines it in terms of Mr. Beara's own words and own terms, I think, best, is P1380, and this is an intercept that is dated 1 August 1995. And this is a conversation between Mr. Beara and a certain Stevo, and in this conversation, they're talking about getting back people that have fled Zepa in order to exchange them. And during the course of the conversation, it reads as follows. This is Stevo speaking: "Hello, Ljubo." And the answer: "Hello, good evening." "Where are you calling from, boss?" "From -- what's this called? "Are you across --" Answer -- or, I'm sorry, reply: "From Cara [phoen]. We there -- now we've just returned. Zoka Cavcic is also with us." This is Beara speaking: "So far, there are about 300 parcels. They, whoever captures a parcel, hands it over to the cops, and now they're keeping that. I've talked to the chief of the SUP from Uzice. He says, 'I can't do anything for you now, but we'll be in touch.' But the chiefs have to make a decision as to what they want to do, so we should tell our chief and the supreme chief, they - this is the information confirmed by my people - they are up to 1.000 parcels in the place like ours, it's all crammed in over there. They said there's some big trouble over there, some commotion and so on, but he says, 'You can't do anything because those are valleys, caves, and nothing can be done there. Small parcels go first and big ones are left for the end, and they'll probably be able -- and they'll probably all go in the same direction.'" That passage speaks volumes as to what that term means, and particularly what that term means when it's used by Ljubo Beara. If we go on to the next page in this intercept, we see what Mr. Beara's involvement is and what his knowledge is concerning the crimes with which he's been charged. What he says is, in respect of the registration of these individuals: "They're taking their names, but that doesn't matter. We can -- you know, we can request the ICRC escort them to us, and they can be exchanged here, as written in the contract. We had no plans to kill them, the mother-fuckers, but to exchange them." This is an important intercept, because what it shows is that he has knowledge that there were plans with respect to the prisoners that preceded the people that he's trying to catch now. When he says, We had no plans to kill them, in the context of an exchange, it means that somebody has reason to think that they do, and he's aware of that. And the reason why he's aware of it, Your Honours, is because he was intimately involved in it. What the Defence has to do or is trying to do in respect of these intercepts in respect of the evidence that comes from the accused's own mouth, is to employ a linguist. That was Mr. Remetic, who came in here to tell you that while the name "Ljubo" is a common name, so you can't rely on the fact that you see that in an intercept in order to identify the accused. All right. He tells you that he's had an opportunity to review these intercepts and is able to discern only from a handful of them that it, in fact, is the accused based upon his dialect, based upon the way he speaks. He testified that he interviewed Mr. Beara for a period of time less than he would have liked to, and it was a relatively short period of time. He testified that he never considered the fact that Mr. Beara was charged with serious offences and serious crimes in order to evaluate whether or not he was being candid and forthright with him, in terms of evaluating his own way of speaking, his manner of speech. He testified that he obtained no speech exemplars or anything that would indicate what Mr. Beara actually sounded like in 1995 to compare against the intercepts that he was evaluating from that period of time. The testimony that he provided to this Trial Chamber is virtually valueless. It is evidence -- or it is information, rather, that the Trial Chamber is perfectly capable of gleaning from the evidence without the expertise, if you want to call it that, that he offers. He can provide no information about the statistical or reliability of his work, no information concerning whether or not it had been peer-reviewed or whether or not it had been evaluated by colleagues, and I would submit that the information that he provided you with is completely valueless. One thing he did say is that the word "senor" is of Roman origin and it is something that is typical -- typically used in Dalmatian speech, and that is the intercept I just read you. That's the one that involves Senor Lucic and shows Beara's involvement in the prisoners in Nova Kasaba. You'll recall that Stefanie Frease also testified to that, testified to the fact that that was a Dalmatian or a typically Dalmatian word. The Beara Defence also seeks to establish this same defence with respect to the word "triage" as is used in this case, and they argue that the word "triage" is used in an intercept, which is 110 -- 1164, and they say that that word means something other than the executions. We know that that particular intercept uses that word almost within a few hours of the commencement of the executions in Pilica. I would submit, and the evidence in this case certainly establishes it -- the evidence of Richard Butler establishes that the term "triage" as is used in this intercept clearly denotes the commencement of the executions that began in Pilica on 16 July. It's important to realise why we say that. One thing we say is because it's very close in time to the commencement of the executions in Pilica. You'll recall that Slavko Peric puts the beginning of those executions at around noon. Drazen Erdemovic also puts them around 10.00 or 11.00. The proximity of the intercept at the time that those executions began certainly suggests the meaning that Mr. Butler has attributed to it in this record. There are also entries in the duty officer log-book -- notebook which I won't go through, but that's another area where the Beara Defence obviously attacks the evidence in this case. That evidence is good, and you've heard testimony about it. You've heard testimony about the chain of custody. You've heard testimony about the nature of the entries that were placed in it. You've heard testimony about the sequential or asynchronous or synchronous writings that are contained in it. And I would submit, Your Honour -- Your Honours, that in evaluating that evidence you will come to the conclusion that it is reliable evidence, and certainly reliable enough to establish the whereabouts and the conduct of the accused in this case. The Defence assert that there is no proof -- there is no proof in this record that Mr. Beara was in Zepa. They said there's not a single witness that claimed to have seen Ljubisa Beara in Zepa, and I assume that that is intended to establish the fact that there's no relation between the crimes that he committed and the forcible transfer of the Zepa population. There's two things that I will note. The first is that the forcible transfer, as is charged in the indictment, includes the men that are transferred to Zvornik; that is, the men that are separated and put on buses in Bratunac and then bussed up to Zvornik to be killed. It is pled as follows under paragraph 78 that states, paragraph A2: "He supervised, facilitated, oversaw the transportation of Muslim men from Potocari to Bratunac and from there to detention centres in the Zvornik area, specifically the schools at Orahovac, Petkovci, Rocevic, Kula, Pilica Cultural Centre, from 13 to 16 July 1995," as part of the forcible transfer in this case. I think the evidence supports Mr. Beara's significant contribution in that sense. The fact is, however, that there is evidence in this case that Mr. Beara was in Zepa, and maybe it's just inadvertence on the part of my colleague, but the record is really rather unambiguous, and it's at transcript 14603, line 22, through 14604, line 7. This is the testimony of PW-109.
